text: Before you go, listen to this. It's music by Johann Sebastian Bach, played on a cello. A cello has four strings. A player presses a string to make the part that plays shorter, and a shorter part sings a higher note. Just like Pythagoras's string. Press play, and press stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. It has three stops. First, learn how to name a fraction. Next, we fix some mix-ups together. Then you try one on your own. Let's begin.
Now it's your turn to work on your own. Use what you learned: equal parts, how many, and of what. You've got this.
These three jobs each have a mix-up that kids often make with fractions. Your job is to find it and fix it. Take your time, and look closely at every part.
Last stop! Show what you know. Remember: a fraction needs equal parts. The bottom number tells how many equal parts make the whole. The top number tells how many parts you're counting.

This is a string over a wooden box, like the one in the stories. First, pluck the whole string and listen. Then slide the two bridges to cut the string into 3 parts. Here's a secret: parts that are the same length sing the same note. Use your ears and your eyes.
You did it! Three parts, all the same length, so they all sing the same note. Each part is one of 3 equal parts. In math, we call that one-third. Hold on to that idea. We'll use it all lesson long.

Hoo, hello! I'm Opti. Come sit with me and open this old book. Each chapter visits a real time and place where people used math. Today's chapter is Ancient Greece, more than 2,500 years ago. Meet Pythagoras. He loved numbers, and he loved music. Stories say he stretched one string over a long wooden box. Then he listened very carefully. Let's listen too.

Before you go, listen to Bach's music on the cello again. A cello player presses each string at just the right spot. The same spot on the string always makes the same note, just like a fraction always lands on the same spot on a number line. Press play, and press stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. It has three stops. First, learn how to draw a number line and put a fraction on it. Next, we fix some mix-ups together. Then you try it on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. This number line keeps going past 1. Count the jumps carefully. Each jump is one unit fraction.
Each of these jobs has a mix-up that kids often make on a number line. Find it and fix it. Count the spaces, not just the marks.
Last stop! Show what you know. Cut the line into equal parts. Count the jumps from 0. Then label the spot.
The string is cut into 5 equal parts. Let's count them out loud together. Tap each bridge, from left to right, and say its name with me. One-fifth. Two-fifths. Keep going, all the way to the end.
Listen to that! Five-fifths is the whole string. Five-fifths is 1. The start of the string is 0, and the end is 1. Each bridge left a tick mark. Our string just became a number line.

Hoo, welcome back! Let's open our old book to the same chapter. We're still in Ancient Greece with Pythagoras and his singing string. Last time, we cut the string into equal parts. Today, the string turns into something new: a number line. Every fraction gets its very own spot.

Before you go, listen to Bach's music on the cello one more time. Listen for the low notes and the high notes. Long parts of a string sing low, and short parts sing high, just like our fractions today. Press play, and press stop whenever you like.

Welcome to the Lesson. It has three stops. First, learn how to compare two fractions with the same denominator and write the answer with a symbol. Next, we fix some mix-ups together. Then you try it on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. On a number line, the fraction farther to the right is greater. Count the jumps from 0 to find each spot.
Each of these jobs has a mix-up that kids often make when they compare fractions. Find it and fix it. Remember: the open side of the symbol always faces the greater fraction.
Last stop! Show what you know. Check that the wholes are the same. Count the equal parts. Then write your answer with a symbol.
Both strings are cut into ninths, so every part is the same size. Slide one bridge to four-ninths and the other bridge to seven-ninths. Then pluck both parts and listen. Which part is longer?
Did you hear it? The longer part sings a lower note. Seven-ninths is more string than four-ninths, because seven parts are more than four parts of the same size. Seven-ninths is greater.

Hoo, welcome back to Chapter 9! Pythagoras now has two strings, side by side. Both strings are the same length, and both are cut into the same number of equal parts. Today, we'll find out which fraction is greater, and we'll even hear the answer.

Before you go, listen to some organ music by Bach. An organ has hundreds of pipes. The long pipes play the low notes, and the short pipes play the high notes. Press play, and press stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. It has three stops. First, learn how to compare fractions that have the same numerator. Next, we fix some mix-ups together and play a tune. Then you try it on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. On two number lines of the same length, count the jumps. Then look at how long each jump is.
Each of these jobs has a mix-up that kids often make. Here's a clue: a bigger denominator does not make a bigger fraction. It means the whole is cut into more pieces, so each piece is smaller.
Last stop! Show what you know. When the numerators match, look at the denominators. Fewer pieces in the whole means bigger pieces.
Both pipes are the same length. Cut the top pipe into nine equal pieces and the bottom pipe into twelve. Then blow one piece of each and listen. Which piece is longer?
Did you hear it? The one-twelfth piece whistled higher, because it is shorter. When you cut the same pipe into more pieces, each piece gets smaller. So one-ninth is greater than one-twelfth.

Hoo, welcome back to Chapter 9! Today Pythagoras has pipes. When you cut a pipe into equal pieces, the pieces can be long or short. We'll find out which fraction is greater when the numerators are the same, and we'll even hear the answer.
Before you go, listen to Bach's music for a group of string players. Hear the long notes and quick notes fit together. Press play, and press stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. It has three stops. First, learn what equivalent fractions are. Next, we fix some mix-ups together. Then you try one on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. Split every piece into two equal pieces. The shaded part stays the same length. Only its name changes.
Each job has a mix-up kids often make. A clue: the wholes must be the same size, and the parts must be equal. Then look at the length, not just the numbers.
Last stop! Show what you know. Fill one of Bach's measures any way you like. Then press Play and listen to your music.
Two players share one measure. The top player plays two one-third notes. Build the bottom row from twelfths until it ends on the same beat. Press Play to check. How many twelfths did it take?
You heard it! Both rows ended on the same beat. Two-thirds and eight-twelfths fill the same amount. In the Lesson, you'll learn a word for this.
Same length, new name. That's what equivalent fractions are. Now it's your turn.

Here is one measure of music. It is one whole. One whole note fills the whole measure. Cut it into two equal parts. Each part is one-half. Let's shade one half. Bach could play a half note here. Now cut every part in half again. There are four equal parts, and two are shaded. That's two-fourths. Two quarter notes take the same time as one half note. Cut every part in half one more time. Eight equal parts, and four are shaded. Four-eighths. Look at the shaded part. It never changed length. One-half, two-fourths, and four-eighths are the same amount. We call them equivalent fractions. Equivalent sounds like equal. They have the same value. Let's check on number lines. One line is in halves, one is in fourths, and one is in eighths. One-half, two-fourths, and four-eighths all land on the same spot. We can go the other way, too. This bar has ten equal parts, and two tenths are shaded. Group the tenths in pairs. Now there are five bigger parts, and one is shaded. Two-tenths is equal to one-fifth. Watch out! Every part must be split or grouped the same way, and the whole must stay the same size. Then the shaded amount stays the same.
Hoo! Claire is going to show us fractions that look different but fill the same amount. Watch the length.

Hoo, welcome to Chapter 10! Let's open our old book to a new time and place: Leipzig, Germany, about 300 years ago. Meet Johann Sebastian Bach. He wrote music, and in his music, one measure is one whole. Bach could fill a measure in many ways: one long note, or shorter notes that take the same time. Let's listen.
Before you go, listen to the Aria that opens Bach's book. It's slow and calm. Listen for the low notes that every variation keeps. Press play, and press stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. First, Claire shows how to find a new name by multiplying. Next, we fix some mix-ups together. Then you try one on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. Find the missing number. Ask yourself, what did I multiply by? Then do the same thing to the other number.
Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. Finding a new name is not adding. Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number. Then check the length.
Last stop! Slide the window along the times table. Every column it stops on is a new name for the same amount. Find three names, then press Play.
Look at one measure cut three ways. The same part is shaded in each row. Count the shaded parts and all the parts in each row, and fill in the table. What do you notice?
You found a pattern! When the parts in all grew two times, the shaded parts grew two times too. Three times, three times. In the Lesson, you'll turn that pattern into a rule.
Same beat, more notes. Multiply both numbers by the same number. Now it's your turn.

Here is one measure. It is one whole. Cut it in half and shade one part. One part is shaded, and there are two parts in all. One-half. Now split every part into two. Two parts are shaded, and there are four parts in all. Both counts doubled. One-half equals two-fourths. Go back to one-half, and split every part into three. Three are shaded, and there are six in all. Both counts are three times as many. One-half equals three-sixths. Split every part into four. Four shaded, eight in all. One-half equals four-eighths. Do you see the rule? Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number. We show it with arrows. Times four on the numerator. Times four on the denominator. The shaded part stays the same length, so the fraction is equivalent. Does it work for thirds, too? Here is two-thirds. Split every part into four. Eight are shaded, and there are twelve in all. Two times four is eight. Three times four is twelve. Two-thirds equals eight-twelfths. Watch out! Always multiply both numbers by the same number. If you change only one, the shaded part changes size.
Hoo! Claire is going to show us how to find equivalent fractions by multiplying. Watch the counts.

Hoo, welcome back to Leipzig! Bach is older now. In 1741, he printed a book of music for the keyboard. It starts with a slow, calm song called the Aria. Then come thirty variations. Each one keeps the Aria's low notes and its measures, but fills the measures with more notes. Same measure, more notes. Today we'll find the math that makes that work.

Before you go, listen to Bach's Sleepers, Wake, played from his music with a soft organ sound. Listen for the slow hymn tune in long notes, with quick notes all around it. Press play, and stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. First, Claire shows how to group parts by dividing. Next, we fix some mix-ups together. Then you try one on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. Find a number that divides both numbers evenly. Divide both. Then check if you can divide again.
Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. Divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number. Don't take away. Then ask, can I divide again?
Last stop! Trade small tiles for bigger ones, two at a time. Keep trading until no bigger tile fits. Then press Play and listen. Fewer notes, longer notes.
Here is one measure cut into ten parts. Eight parts are shaded. Can you shade the same amount on a strip with fewer parts? Try the halves. Then try the fifths. Which one lines up?
You found it! Eight-tenths and four-fifths are the same amount. The fifths strip has fewer parts, and each part is bigger. More parts does not mean more music.
Fewer, longer notes. Divide both numbers by the same number, until you can't anymore. Now it's your turn.

Here is a measure cut into ten parts. Eight are shaded. That's eight-tenths. Now group the parts in twos. Every two small parts make one bigger part. Count again. Four parts are shaded, and there are five in all. Eight divided by two is four. Ten divided by two is five. Eight-tenths equals four-fifths. Line up the two strips. The shaded parts are the same length. Here is sixteen-twentieths. Sofia divides both numbers by two, and gets eight-tenths. She divides by two again, and gets four-fifths. Small steps. Alex sees that four divides both numbers. Sixteen divided by four is four. Twenty divided by four is five. Four-fifths, in one big step. Both ways land in the same place. Can we divide four and five by the same number? Only by one. So four-fifths is in simplest form. It has the fewest, biggest parts. Watch out! Divide both numbers by the same number. If you divide only one number, or take away, the shaded part changes size.
Hoo! Claire is going to show us how to find a simpler name for a fraction by dividing. Watch the parts.

Hoo, welcome back to Leipzig! It's 1731, and Bach has written new music for church called Sleepers, Wake. In one part, the violins play a quick, dancing tune full of short notes. The singers sing an old hymn tune in long, slow notes. One long note fills the same time as a group of short ones. Fewer notes, longer notes. Today we'll find the math in that.
Simplify. ... Simplest form.

Before you go, listen to Bach's first Invention, one of the pieces he wrote for students like Friedemann. Listen for the two parts, one for each hand, chasing each other up and down. Press play, and stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. First, Claire shows two ways to compare. Next, we fix some mix-ups together. Then you try one on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. Re-cut one fraction so both have the same denominator. Then count the pieces and compare.
Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. Before you compare, re-cut so both fractions have the same size pieces. Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number.
Last stop! Press Play and listen to both parts together. Which note keeps ringing after the other one stops? Then re-cut and count to prove what you heard.
Here are two parts in one measure. One note lasts four-fifths of the measure. The other lasts seven-tenths. They look almost the same! Cut each fifth into two pieces. Then count and compare.
You did it! Four-fifths is the same as eight-tenths. Now both parts are cut into tenths, so you can count. Eight tenths is more than seven tenths. Same-size pieces make comparing fair.
Same-size pieces make comparing fair. Re-cut, then count. Now it's your turn.

Here are four-fifths and seven-tenths. The bars are the same length, but the pieces are different sizes. So we can't just count yet. Let's re-cut. Cut each fifth into two pieces. Now both bars have tenths. Four-fifths is eight-tenths. Four times two is eight. Five times two is ten. Look, the shaded parts still line up. Re-cutting didn't change the amount. Eight-tenths is more than seven-tenths, so four-fifths is greater. That's Dion's way. He makes a common denominator. Emma has another way. Here are one-sixth and two-elevenths. She makes the numerators match. One-sixth is two-twelfths. Now both have two pieces. A twelfth is smaller than an eleventh. So two-elevenths is greater. That's a common numerator. Watch out! Don't compare only the numerators, or only the denominators. Re-cut first, so the pieces are the same size. Then compare.
Hoo! Claire is going to show us two ways to compare fractions with different denominators. Watch the pieces.

Hoo, hello again! Before Bach moved to Leipzig, he started a little music book for his son Friedemann, who was nine years old. Inside are short pieces with two parts, one for each hand. Later, Bach wrote them out neatly and called them Inventions. Two hands play in the same measure. Which part holds its note longer? Today we'll find out.
Common denominator. ... Common numerator. ... Re-cut.

Before you go, listen to Lieschen's song from the Coffee Cantata. She sings about how sweet her coffee tastes, and a flute plays along. It's played here with a soft flute and harpsichord sound. Press play, and stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. First, Claire shows two shortcuts: the halfway line and the missing piece. Next, we fix some mix-ups. Then you try one on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. Find half of each denominator. Is each fraction less than half, or more? Then compare.
Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. Half of an odd number has a half in it. And when both fractions are past the halfway line, look at the missing pieces.
Last stop! Sort the coffee cups. Less than half full goes on the left of the halfway line. More than half full goes on the right. Then press Play.
Here are three cups of coffee. Each cup is one whole. Press the button to show the halfway line. Which cups are more than half full? Which one is closest to full?
Nice work! Two cups are past the halfway line. Nine-tenths is missing just one small piece, so it is closest to full. You compared without re-cutting!
Halfway line, or missing piece. Pick the shortcut that helps. Now it's your turn.

Here are two-ninths and five-sevenths. Each cup is one whole. Let's draw a line at one-half. Half of nine is four and a half. Two-ninths is less than that, so it's less than one-half. Half of seven is three and a half. Five-sevenths is more than that, so it's more than one-half. So five-sevenths is greater. One-half is a benchmark. It's a number we compare to. Now here are nine-tenths and eleven-twelfths. Both are more than one-half, so the halfway line can't help. Look at the missing pieces instead. Each cup is missing one piece. A twelfth is smaller than a tenth. So eleven-twelfths is closer to full. Eleven-twelfths is greater. Watch out! Half of an odd number has a half in it. And the cup with the smaller missing piece is closer to one whole.
Hoo! Claire is going to show us two shortcuts for comparing fractions. Watch the halfway line.

Hoo, welcome to a coffee house in Leipzig! About three hundred years ago, people came here to drink coffee and hear music. Bach's music group often played here. Bach wrote a funny piece called the Coffee Cantata. A father wants his daughter Lieschen to stop drinking coffee. But she loves it! Today we'll look at cups of coffee. Is a cup less than half full, more than half full, or almost full?
Benchmark. ... One-half. ... Cantata.

Before you go, listen to a little piece from Anna Magdalena's notebook. It's a musette, a happy dance. Nobody knows for sure who wrote it. It's played here with a harpsichord sound. Press play, and stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. First, Claire shows how to add and take away pieces that are the same size. Next, we fix some mix-ups. Then you try one on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. Find the unit first. Take away one amount, and then take away the other.
Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. The denominator tells the size of the pieces. When you add or take away pieces, they don't change size.
Last stop! Each measure needs sixteen sixteenths. Some notes are already written. Add sixteenths until each measure is full. Then press Play.
Anna Magdalena is copying one measure. It holds sixteen sixteenth notes. She writes five, then nine more. How much of the measure is written now? Then a drop of ink smudges three notes.
You did it! Five sixteenths and nine sixteenths make fourteen sixteenths. Take away three, and eleven sixteenths are left. Sixteenths are the unit, so you just count them.
Same-size pieces? Count them, and keep the unit. Now it's your turn.

Four apples plus three apples is seven apples. Fractions work the same way. Here is one whole, cut into ninths. Four-ninths are shaded. Now add three more ninths. Count on: five, six, seven. Four-ninths plus three-ninths equals seven-ninths. Ninths are the unit. We counted ninths, so the answer is still in ninths. Now let's take some away. Start at seven-ninths on the number line. Take away five-ninths. Hop back five: six, five, four, three, two. We land on two-ninths. Seven-ninths minus five-ninths equals two-ninths. Watch out! Don't add the denominators. The pieces are still ninths, so the denominator stays nine. And to take away from one whole, cut it into pieces first. One whole is nine-ninths.
Hoo! Claire is going to show us how to add and take away fractions. Watch the size of the pieces.

Hoo, it's Saturday night in Leipzig, about three hundred years ago. Tomorrow, Bach's choir will sing a brand-new cantata. But every singer and every player needs their own part, copied by hand! So Anna Magdalena Bach and Bach's students copy music late into the night. Every measure has to add up to one whole. Today you'll add pieces of a measure, and take some away.
Unit. ... Sum. ... Difference. ... Copyist.

The cantata is over, and our chapter ends here. Listen to a chorale from a Bach cantata first sung in Leipzig in 1723. Today we call it Jesu, Joy of Man's Desiring. This is a real recording. Press play, and stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. First, Claire shows how clue words tell you to add or take away. Next, we fix some mix-ups. Then you try one on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. Read the story, find the clue words, and do one step at a time.
Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. Read the whole story before you start. How much more means find the gap between two amounts.
Last stop! Now you're the writer. Pick a clue word, build two amounts, and write your own Sunday story. Then solve it.
Here's the first fix. The trumpet part has three sixteenths written. The copyist writes eleven more. Then Bach scratches out five wrong notes. Look for the clue words.
Nice work! Three sixteenths and eleven more make fourteen sixteenths. Scratch out five, and nine sixteenths are left. More told you to add. Scratches out told you to take away.
Read the whole story, find the clue words, then do one step at a time. Now it's your turn!

Read the whole story first. Here's one. Lena has two-elevenths of a meter of ribbon. She adds seven-elevenths more. Then she cuts off four-elevenths. Adds more means add. Two-elevenths plus seven-elevenths is nine-elevenths. Cuts off means take away. Nine-elevenths minus four-elevenths is five-elevenths. Do one step at a time, and keep elevenths the unit. Now a different clue. One candle is six-sevenths of a foot tall. The other is one-seventh of a foot. How much taller is the first candle? How much more, or how much taller, means find the gap. Line up the two bars. Count the extra pieces: one, two, three, four, five. The first candle is five-sevenths of a foot taller. We found the gap, so we took away. We did not add. Watch out! Check if your answer can be simpler. One-twelfth plus one-twelfth is two-twelfths. Two twelfths fit exactly under one sixth. So the simplest form is one-sixth.
Hoo! Claire is going to show us how clue words tell you what to do. Listen for them.

Hoo, it's Sunday morning in Leipzig, about three hundred years ago. The bells of Saint Thomas Church are ringing. Today Bach's choir and players will perform the cantata they copied all week. Look at the old picture. Singers and players crowd into a church loft, just like this. But first, a few last fixes! Today you'll add and take away, one step at a time.
Altogether. ... How much more. ... Clue word.

Our first day in Paris ends here. Listen to music by Joseph Haydn. It was first played in London in 1794, while people were measuring France. People call it the Clock, because it goes tick, tock, tick, tock, steady as the marks on a meter stick. Press play, and stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. First, Claire shows how meters and centimeters fit together. Next, we fix some mix-ups. Then you measure on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. Remember, each meter is one hundred centimeters. Take your time.
Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. Always start measuring at zero. And before you compare two lengths, write them in the same unit.
Last stop! Now you get to cut the ribbon. Make it just the right length, then check it on the marble meter.
Here's your first check. This cloth is longer than one meter stick. Lay the meter stick at the end of the cloth first. Then measure the rest with the small ruler.
You did it! The cloth is one meter and thirty-seven centimeters long. One meter is one hundred centimeters, so that's also one hundred thirty-seven centimeters. Same cloth, two ways to say it.
Meters are hundreds of centimeters. Start at zero, and say it both ways. Now it's your turn!

This is a meter stick. It is one meter long. Look at the tiny spaces. Each one is one centimeter. Let's count them by tens. Ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety, one hundred. One meter is one hundred centimeters. Here's a rope. It is longer than one meter stick. Lay the meter stick at the end of the rope. That's one meter. Measure the rest with a centimeter ruler, starting at zero. It's forty-six centimeters. So the rope is one meter forty-six centimeters. In centimeters, that's one hundred plus forty-six, or one hundred forty-six centimeters. Now go the other way. A garden path is nine hundred thirty-five centimeters long. How many meters? Every hundred centimeters makes one meter. Nine hundreds make nine meters. Thirty-five centimeters are left over. So the path is nine meters thirty-five centimeters. Watch out! Eight meters three centimeters is not eighty-three centimeters. Eight meters is eight hundred centimeters. Add three more, and you get eight hundred three centimeters.
Hoo! Claire is going to show us how meters and centimeters fit together. Watch the meter stick.

Hoo! It's Paris, France, in the year 1796. Workers are setting a long marble stone into a wall. Carved on it is something new, one meter. Shopkeepers can come and check their measuring sticks against it. Look at the old picture. A man measures cloth with a meter stick. Today you'll measure with meters and centimeters, and say one length two ways.
Meter. ... Centimeter. ... Length. ... Meter stick.

The shop is closing for the night. Listen to music by Joseph Haydn, first played in London in 1792. It's soft and quiet, and then, surprise, one big loud chord! Stories say he wanted to wake up sleepy listeners. Press play, and stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. First, Claire shows two ways to take centimeters away from meters. Next, we fix some mix-ups. Then you cut an order on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. Take away the meters first. Then break a meter for the centimeters.
Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. Break only one meter, and keep the other meters. Then check by adding back.
Last stop! The orders are coming in. Cut each one from the roll, and say what's left.
Here's the first order. The roll has nine whole meters. The customer wants forty-seven centimeters. You can't cut centimeters from a whole meter, so break one meter first.

Well done! You broke one meter into one hundred centimeters. You cut off forty-seven, and fifty-three were left. Eight whole meters are still on the roll. So eight meters fifty-three centimeters remain.
Break one meter, keep the rest, and check by adding back. Now it's your turn!

A ribbon roll has nine meters. A customer wants twenty-eight centimeters. We can't take centimeters from a whole meter. So break one meter into one hundred centimeters. Now we have eight meters and one hundred centimeters. Take twenty-eight from the hundred. Count up from twenty-eight: two more makes thirty, and seventy more makes one hundred. Two and seventy is seventy-two. So seventy-two centimeters are left, and the eight meters are still there. Nine meters minus twenty-eight centimeters is eight meters seventy-two centimeters. Here's another way. Take away one whole meter. That leaves eight meters. But we only needed twenty-eight centimeters, so we took too much. Give back the extra seventy-two centimeters. Eight meters and seventy-two centimeters again. Watch out! Don't forget to break a meter. Nine meters minus twenty-eight centimeters is not nine meters seventy-two centimeters. One of the nine meters was broken, so only eight are left.
Hoo! Claire is going to show us how to take centimeters away from meters. Watch the meter break.

Hoo! It's the day after we saw the marble meter. Now we're in a ribbon shop in Paris. The rolls of ribbon are measured in whole meters. But customers ask for pieces in centimeters. Look at the old picture of a busy Paris shop, full of ribbons and cloth. Today you'll cut pieces off whole meters and find out how much is left.
Subtract. ... Remaining. ... Break a meter. ... Compound units.

Here's music from about the same time as the towers. It's a slow part of a symphony by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, written in 1780. Listen to the strings, soft and smooth, like a signal passing from tower to tower. Press play, and stop whenever you like.
Welcome to the Lesson. First, Claire shows how meters build up to kilometers. Next, we fix some mix-ups. Then you work on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. Find the thousands first. Those are the kilometers.
Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. A kilometer is one thousand meters, not one hundred. And always compare in the same unit.
Last stop! A message has to reach three stops along a road. Move it to each one, and say how far it went.
Before the test, a messenger runs a note from the workshop up to the tower. The path is one thousand nine hundred meters long. Build it out of hundred-meter pieces, and watch what happens at ten.
You did it! Ten pieces of one hundred meters made one kilometer. Nine more pieces made nine hundred meters. So one thousand nine hundred meters is one kilometer nine hundred meters.
Ten hundreds make a thousand, and a thousand meters make a kilometer. Now it's your turn!

Here is a road made of pieces. Each piece is one hundred meters long. Let's count by hundreds: one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, and so on, all the way to one thousand. Ten pieces of one hundred meters make one thousand meters. One thousand meters is one kilometer. A kilometer is about a fifteen-minute walk. Now let's build a longer road, three thousand four hundred meters long. Every ten pieces make a kilometer, so we have three kilometers. Four pieces are left over. That's four hundred meters. Three thousand four hundred meters is three kilometers four hundred meters. To go the other way, think of every kilometer as one thousand meters. Three kilometers four hundred meters is three thousand meters and four hundred meters, so three thousand four hundred meters. Watch out! A kilometer is not one hundred meters. Six kilometers is six thousand meters, not six hundred meters.
Hoo! Claire is going to show us how meters add up to kilometers. Watch the road grow.

Hoo! It's Paris in the summer of 1793. On the highest hill in the city, Claude Chappe and his brothers built a wooden tower with arms that move. Each way the arms point stands for a signal. Far away, another tower watches through a telescope and copies the signal. Look at the old picture of their test. Today you'll measure long distances in kilometers and meters.

Welcome to the Lesson. First, Claire shows how to break a kilometer. Next, we fix some mix-ups. Then you work on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. Take away the whole kilometers first. Then break one kilometer for the meters.
Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. A kilometer breaks into one thousand meters, not one hundred. And once you break it, that kilometer is gone.
Last stop! A road gets measured in two parts. Cut off each part, one after the other, and say how much road is left each time.
Today the team has three kilometers of road to measure. By lunch, they have measured four hundred fifty meters. How much road is left? Break a kilometer to find out.

You did it! You broke one kilometer into one thousand meters and cut off four hundred fifty. Five hundred fifty meters were left, plus two whole kilometers. So two kilometers five hundred fifty meters of road are left.
Break a kilometer into one thousand meters, then take away. Now it's your turn!

Here is a road six kilometers long. We need to take away one kilometer two hundred forty meters. First, take away the whole kilometer. Now five kilometers are left. Next, we need two hundred forty meters, but every piece here is a whole kilometer. So we break one kilometer. One kilometer is one thousand meters. Now we have four kilometers and one thousand meters. Cut off two hundred forty meters. One thousand minus two hundred forty is seven hundred sixty. So four kilometers seven hundred sixty meters are left. You can also use numbers. Six kilometers is six thousand meters. One kilometer two hundred forty meters is one thousand two hundred forty meters. Six thousand minus one thousand two hundred forty is four thousand seven hundred sixty meters. That's four kilometers seven hundred sixty meters, the same answer. Watch out! A broken kilometer is one thousand meters, not one hundred. And once you break it, that kilometer is gone. Count what's left in whole kilometers.

Hoo! It's France in 1798. Jean-Baptiste Delambre and his team are measuring the land to find out how long a meter should be. Near the town of Melun, they measure a straight road almost twelve kilometers long. They lay metal rulers end to end, again and again. Look at an old picture of a team doing the same kind of job. Today you'll subtract meters from kilometers.

Welcome to the Lesson. First, Claire shows how to read a beaker and fill a liter. Next, we fix some mix-ups. Then you work on your own.
Your turn to work on your own. Read the beaker carefully. Then read a thermometer. It has marks too, and they tell how hot or cold it is.
Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. Before you count, find what each little mark is worth. And one liter is one thousand milliliters, just like a kilometer is one thousand meters.
Last stop! Pour two beakers into one liter bottle. The bottle fills up before the second beaker is empty. Then say how much there is in liters and milliliters.
A milk seller has a big jug of milk. She pours it into a beaker to measure it. Read the marks to find how much milk there is. Then pour it into liter bottles.

You did it! The beaker showed one thousand eight hundred fifty milliliters. One thousand filled a liter bottle, and eight hundred fifty were left. So the seller has one liter eight hundred fifty milliliters of milk.
Find what each mark is worth. One thousand milliliters fill one liter. Now it's your turn!

Here is a beaker. It holds one thousand milliliters. Each small mark is fifty milliliters, so count by fifties. Fifty, one hundred, one hundred fifty, two hundred. The water is at six hundred milliliters. Pour in more, up to the top. Now there are one thousand milliliters. Pour it into this bottle. It's full. One thousand milliliters fill one liter. Now the beaker has one thousand three hundred fifty milliliters. Pour it into an empty bottle. The bottle fills up, and three hundred fifty milliliters are left. So one thousand three hundred fifty milliliters is one liter three hundred fifty milliliters. To go back, one liter is one thousand milliliters, plus three hundred fifty. Watch out! Six liters forty milliliters is six thousand forty milliliters. Not six hundred forty, and not six thousand four hundred. Each liter is one thousand milliliters.
Hoo! Claire is going to show us how to read a beaker and fill a liter. Watch the water rise.

Hoo! It's Paris in 1795. France has a brand-new way to measure milk, water and juice. It's called the liter. Shopkeepers put away their old pint pots and pour with new liter measures instead. In this old picture, a man pours through a funnel to fill a bottle. Today you'll read the marks on a beaker and see how milliliters fill a liter.

Your turn to work on your own. Find what each mark on the dial is worth. Then change kilograms to grams.
Each job has a mix-up kids often make. Here's a clue. One kilogram is one thousand grams. Write both weights in grams before you compare them.
Last stop! A box sits on one side of a balance. Add weights to the other side until the two sides are level. Then you'll know how heavy the box is.
Lavoisier's helpers fill a jar with water and set it on a scale. Read the dial to find how heavy it is. Then write it in kilograms and grams.
You did it! The pointer passed one kilogram and went nine more marks. Each mark is one hundred grams, so the jar weighs one thousand nine hundred grams. That's one kilogram nine hundred grams.
One kilogram is one thousand grams. Find what each mark is worth. Now it's your turn!

Here is a scale. Each small mark on the dial is one hundred grams. A bag of flour sits on the scale. The pointer is three marks past zero, so the bag weighs three hundred grams. Add a five hundred gram weight and a two hundred gram weight. Now the pointer is at one thousand grams. One thousand grams is one kilogram. Now a bag of potatoes is on the scale. The pointer passes one kilogram and goes seven more marks. That's one thousand seven hundred grams, or one kilogram seven hundred grams. To go back, one kilogram is one thousand grams, plus seven hundred. Watch out! Seven kilograms sixty grams is seven thousand sixty grams. Not seven hundred sixty, and not seven thousand six hundred. Each kilogram is one thousand grams.

Hoo! It's France in the 1790s. Scientists want new weights that are the same everywhere. Antoine Lavoisier, a chemist with a very careful balance, helps plan them. The idea is simple. A gram is the weight of a tiny cube of water, one centimeter on each side. A thousand grams make a kilogram. Look at an old painting of Lavoisier at his table of glass and brass tools. Today you'll weigh things in kilograms and grams.

Last stop! First, pour some water. Then weigh it in a bucket. Remember, one milliliter of water weighs one gram. Then solve the problem.
A cloth seller at the market has five meters of cloth. She sells two meters forty-eight centimeters. Cut the cloth to find out how much she has left.
You did it! You handed over two meters, broke a meter into one hundred centimeters, and cut forty-eight. Two meters fifty-two centimeters of cloth are left.
Read it, draw it, convert, then solve and write it the tidy way. Now it's your turn!

Here is a word problem. A rope is six meters twenty centimeters long. Ben cuts off two meters fifty-five centimeters, then one meter seventy centimeters. How much rope is left? Step one, read it and find the question. Step two, draw a bar model. The whole bar is six meters twenty centimeters. The two pieces are parts. The part that's left is the question mark. Step three, convert to one unit and solve. Six meters twenty centimeters is six hundred twenty centimeters. Six hundred twenty minus two hundred fifty-five is three hundred sixty-five. Minus one hundred seventy is one hundred ninety-five. Step four, write it in compound units: one meter ninety-five centimeters. The same steps work for liters. A jug has two liters three hundred fifty milliliters of juice. Mia pours out one liter seven hundred sixty milliliters. Two thousand three hundred fifty minus one thousand seven hundred sixty is five hundred ninety milliliters. Watch out! Three meters one hundred ten centimeters is not finished. One hundred ten centimeters is one more meter and ten centimeters. Write four meters ten centimeters.

Hoo! It's Paris in the year 1800. The new measures are everywhere now. Look at this old print. A man pours with a liter. A woman weighs with grams on a balance. You found the center! Every line from the center to the edge was eleven centimeters long. And both folds went right through the center.
